newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European businesses calm about Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: European businesses calm about Hong Kong handover.

text.p: European businesses are taking the handover of Hong Kong to China in their stride, expecting little change in the investment climate and perhaps even greater opportunities for links with the mainland.

The British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, just 100 days away on Sunday. Although questions remain about Beijing's administration of Hong Kong, there is little sign of a mass exodus of European investment.
Indeed, many European firms see the changeover as a chance to increase their penetration of the potentially huge Chinese market.

"The vast, vast, vast majority consider Hong Kong as the key entry point for their China business ... The vast majority would like to increase their own activities," Ekkehard Goetting of the German Federation of Chambers of Commerce said this week.
He noted that German businesses had increased their presence in Hong Kong by about 20 percent over the past five years.

Federico Galdi, of Italy's industrial employers' federation Confindustria, said business would worry if China began pushing back economic liberalism but that was not expected. "We think Beijing wants to make Hong Kong work," he said.
Like Goetting, Galdi said Hong Kong would be a staging post for companies seeking a way into the mainland market, particularly the lucrative region closest to the colony.
"Hong Kong is an instrument for industrial and commercial penetration in southern China," he said.
Giuseppe Morchio, chairman of Pirelli Cavi, the cable division of the Pirelli group, agreed that Beijing was unlikely to do anything to jeopardise Hong Kong's attractiveness to foreign investors.
"China has a big interest in keeping Hong Kong successful," he said. "With the contacts we have, we do not see any problems arising."
There was little evidence that companies with a presence in Hong Kong were considering a move.
"We have no indication that Dutch companies are planning to leave Hong Kong or have already done so," said George Ammerlaan, Amsterdam director of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council.

He said the Netherlands had two-way trade of about US$3.9 billion with Hong Kong in the 10 months to October 1996. Companies with business in the colony include Royal Dutch/Shell, Unilever, Heineken and banks ANB AMRO and ING.
Marc Ronca, president of the Swiss-Chinese Chamber of Commerce, said that if there was any movement of firms out of Hong Kong, it appeared to be towards China rather than away from it.

"I rather see a tendency to go from Hong Kong to Shanghai for certain companies because part of the action, particularly in manufacturing, will develop more strongly in the Shanghai area than around Hong Kong," he said.
Many companies already do not differentiate between the colony and China.
In Stockholm, spokesmen for telecommunications company Ericsson and appliance maker Electrolux both said their companies treated Hong Kong and China as one market.
"We are not planning to initiate any changes from our side but we will have to adapt our organisation according to developments," Ericsson's Lars Stalberg said.

"It's an integrated business area in the sense that we have a subsidiary listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange and that company owns our activities in China," a spokesman for Danish shipping and trading group East Asiatic Company said.
But the handover of Hong Kong to China will afford one group of European businesses an opportunity not available to others.
Mario Matos dos Santos, economic consultant to the Macau mission in Lisbon, said firms in the Portuguese colony would be able to see how the transition went before worrying about their own.
"Businesses will watch events in Hong Kong as a barometer for Portugal's handover of Macau to China in 1999," he said.
